newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong culture icons fade on Chinese mainland.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong culture icons fade on Chinese mainland.

text.p: The icons of Hong Kong popular culture who once dominated the attention of China's youth and karaoke afficianados, are fading just as the territory prepares to return to the Motherland's embrace.

The Cantonese pop stars of Hong Kong generated extravagant adulation in Shanghai and elsewhere on the Chinese mainland for more than a decade, but are now increasingly met with yawns from a jaded public.

The thousands of karaoke hangouts which two years ago dominated Shanghai nightlife, have shrunk in number and the crooners of old are now often found spending their cash in bowling alleys, bars and coffee houses instead.

"Some of the Cantonese pop singers are still quite popular, especially Jackie Cheung and Andy Lau, but it's not like a couple of years ago," said an official at Shanghai's cable music television station. "Let's face it, they're getting old."
The Hong Kong pop machine has so far failed to produce any serious contenders for the mantle slipping from the shoulders of the "Four Heavenly Kings" of Canto-pop -- Jackie, Andy, Aaron and Leon.
And the songs are not as memorable as they once were, fans say.

"People have started to realise that all the Hong Kong songs are much the same -- I love you, you love me -- there's no cultural depth or sophistication to the music at all," said a one-time karaoke fan who now rarely picks up a microphone.

The Hong Kong cultural invasion of China began after 1980 when the country started to open its doors and found waiting on its doorstep a mature pop music machine pumping out Chinese tunes influenced by both Western and Japanese pop music.

They swept the nation, even though the songs were mostly sung in Cantonese -- the Chinese dialect used in Hong Kong and nearby Guangdong province which is very different from the national Chinese dialect, Mandarin.

But as gargantuan China prepares to resume rule over Hong Kong on July 1, ending the territory's 156 years of British colonial rule, Cantonese doesn't appear to have much of a future on the national Chinese scene.

"Interest in Cantonese language pop songs is gradually fading, that's the way the market is moving," said Fang Jian, a manager of Shanghai's largest karaoke complex, the Taiwan-owned Cashbox. "The requirement for Mandarin is growing."
"Many Hong Kong pop stars are now putting out their albums in Mandarin," said the Shanghai Music TV official.
"It's all part of the return of Hong Kong to China. If you want to break into the mainland market, you've got to do Mandarin."
Another factor, say fans, is the growing sense of confidence in China and its own cultural base.
Some local mainland artists, such as Mao Ning, Gao Linsheng and Li Cu, are also emerging to fill part of the vacuum left by the deflating stars of Canto-pop.

"A national pride in being Chinese is growing which excites interest in local singers," said one fan. "There's a much more powerful feel to the music of the new mainland singers, a much more mainland feel."
